Storm May Not Provide Relief for Insurance Market
 
Also, Fed’s Hammack eyes higher interest rates and Trump’s industrial promises face big tests
 
 
GILLES SABRIÉ FOR WSJ
 

A generation born during China’s boom years is now entering adulthood with dwindling opportunities, fiercer competition and a growing sense of despondency that years of hard work have left them no better off than their parents—and, for some, back living with them. Steady jobs are hard to get, pushing millions into the precarious gig economy, while others buckle under a cutthroat work culture.

 

A weakened economy has shrunk the job market, just as record numbers of college graduates are looking to start their careers. The rapid adoption of AI is adding to the uncertainty.

 

Many top employers, including tech giants Alibaba and ByteDance, have been quietly cutting staff. Although the companies aren’t publicly blaming AI, the technology has been a factor, people familiar with the matter say. Other industries, from filmmaking to finance, are using AI to scale back hiring.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

 
 
 

Planning & Investing

 

Gulf Hurricane Not Big Enough to Reset Insurance Market

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

European banks have strong fundamentals at attractive valuations after underperforming the broader market by 7% on concerns around rising sovereign bond yields, J.P. Morgan analysts write. As a result, JPM maintains its positive view on the continent’s banks. The discount of European banks to the market is back at 31%, which JPM doesn’t think is justified based on improvement to sector fundamentals and relatively high confidence in their earnings trajectory of. JPM retains its overweight recommendation on European banks. It adds Julius Baer to its existing top picks of UBS, Deutsche Bank, ING Groep, NatWest and Standard Chartered after enforcement proceedings against the Swiss bank concluded. (michael.hennessey@wsj.com)

 

Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee says the ultimate settling place for interest rates is a someplace a fair bit below where we are now. In an interview published by Semafor, Goolsbee says rates can come down if the Fed gets evidence that inflation is on a path back to 2% with full employment. “But the more you see services inflation going up and the more you see AI demand jumping out of its lane and overheating the rest of the economy, then it’s going to be a little dicier,” he says. (jessica.coacci@wsj.com)
